content: The enzyme CYP3A4 is involved in the metabolism of certain drugs. It is recommended to avoid or use alternative medications when interactions with this enzyme are a concern. Severe and potentially fatal hepatitis can occur within the first three months of treatment and may also develop months after treatment has ended. The risk of hepatitis is age-related and increases with daily alcohol consumption. Patients should be educated about the signs and symptoms of hepatitis. Hypersensitivity reactions to isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and rifamycins can occur. Acute liver disease, severe hepatic damage, and acute gout are contraindications for these medications. Rifampin is contraindicated in patients receiving ritonavir-boosted saquinavir due to an increased risk of severe hepatocellular toxicity. Many CYP substrates are contraindicated with rifampin because of the risk of decreased systemic exposure. Rifampin is also contraindicated with atazanavir, darunavir, fosamprenavir, saquinavir, or tipranavir, as it can significantly reduce plasma concentrations of these antiviral drugs, potentially leading to loss of antiviral efficacy for HIV infection and/or the development of viral resistance. Systemic hypersensitivity reactions, including Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS) syndrome, may occur. Symptoms of these reactions can include fever, rash, urticaria, angioedema, hypotension, acute bronchospasm, conjunctivitis, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, elevated liver transaminases, or flu-like symptoms (e.g., weakness, fatigue, muscle pain, nausea, vomiting, headache, chills, aches, itching, sweats, dizziness, shortness of breath, chest pain, cough, syncope, palpitations). Patients should avoid foods containing tyramine and histamine (e.g., skipjack, tuna, and other tropical fish) while on therapy. The reliability of oral or other systemic hormonal contraceptives may be reduced by rifampin. Alternative contraceptive measures should be considered. Patients should abstain from alcohol, hepatotoxic medications, or herbal products while receiving therapy. Emphasize the importance of completing the full course of therapy and not missing any doses. Monitor for symptoms and clinical or laboratory signs of liver injury, especially if treatment is prolonged or combined with other hepatotoxic drugs. Rifampin should only be used in patients with impaired liver function when absolutely necessary and under strict medical supervision. Liver function should be carefully monitored prior to therapy and every 2–4 weeks during therapy. If signs of hepatic damage occur or worsen, rifampin should be discontinued. Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCAR), such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), and acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP), have been reported. If symptoms or signs of severe cutaneous adverse reactions develop, discontinue rifampin immediately and initiate appropriate therapy. Rifampin may cause vitamin K–dependent coagulation disorders and bleeding. Coagulation tests (e.g., prothrombin time and other coagulation parameters) should be monitored during rifampin treatment in patients at risk of vitamin K deficiency (e.g., those with chronic liver disease, poor nutritional status, or on prolonged antibacterial drugs or anticoagulants). Therapy should be discontinued if abnormal coagulation tests and/or bleeding occur. Supplemental vitamin K administration should be considered when appropriate. Postmarketing reports suggest that concomitant administration of high doses of cefazolin and rifampin may prolong prothrombin time, leading to severe vitamin K–dependent coagulation disorders that may be life-threatening or fatal. Concomitant use of cefazolin and rifampin should be avoided in patients at increased risk for bleeding. If no alternative treatment options are available, closely monitor prothrombin time and other coagulation tests, and administer vitamin K as indicated. Isoniazid has been reported to have embryocidal effects in rats and rabbits, although no congenital abnormalities have been observed in mammalian offspring when administered during pregnancy. Pyrazinamide has not been studied in animal reproductive studies. Isoniazid is known to be secreted into breast milk. Due to the potential for tumorigenicity shown for rifampin in animal studies, a decision should be made whether to discontinue nursing or discontinue the drug, taking into account the importance of the drug to the mother. Category A: Generally acceptable. Controlled studies in pregnant women show no evidence of fetal risk.
